entries.verbatim: Adjust Chip Load to account for neck length to cutter diameter ratio. (see Table 2)
entries.frame_note: The step text says 'cutter diameter'; the worked example divides by neck diameter (.500 / .076). The printed table is 'Table 1' (the step says Table 2). Record both as printed.

entries.verbatim: Neck Length Ratio = (Neck Length / Neck Diameter)
entries.frame_note: Axis = neck length / NECK diameter of a lollipop undercutting end mill; base 100 % is 5x (3x is a boost to 120 %). entries.verbatim: For Long and Extra Carbide Reduce Feed by 50%.
entries.frame_note: Printed under 'PROFILING CUTTING DEPTH RECOMMENDATIONS AND ADJUSTMENTS'. The chart does not define Long or Extra as an L/D. Host is a forum mirror.

entries.verbatim: (4) For extra long endmills, reduce SFM by 25%.
entries.applies_to: surface speed (SFM), not feed per tooth
entries.frame_note: A speed factor. At a fixed chip load it lowers the feed rate by the same 25 %, but the chip load per tooth is unchanged.

entries.verbatim: Reduce feed rates by 20% when using long length tools.
entries.frame_note: Footnote under several HP/XHP tables in the same document.

entries.verbatim: (4) The use of Long and Extra Long Endmills require a reduction in feed by up to 50%.
entries.frame_note: 'up to 50%': a ceiling on the reduction, not a value.

entries.verbatim: Milling Long Reach or with Long Overhang / Reduce speed and chipload / by 10%
entries.axis_value: long reach or long overhang (undefined L/D)
entries.frame_note: Page 5 is a diagram page; the layout text is garbled, the raw text is readable. Within one vendor document the long-tool rule varies from 10 % to 'up to 50 %'.

entries.verbatim: For extra long end mills the SFM should be reduced by 25%.
entries.frame_note: Same wording family as RedLine p216. A speed factor, not a chip-load factor.

entries.verbatim: Tool overhang length decreases rigidity as a third power (L3), but even more importantly, tool diameter increases rigidity by the
entries.frame_note: Rigidity ~ D^4 / L^3 (the sentence ends 'fourth power (D4).' on the next layout line). This is the cantilever law that feeds::force / tool_load deflection already uses; it is a second witness for the model, not a factor.

entries.verbatim: essential to look at necked-down tooling when reaching >3x dia. depths.
entries.frame_note: A tooling choice threshold at 3x diameter, with no feed factor.

entries.verbatim: In theory, doubling the length sticking out of the holder will result in 8 times more deflection. Doubling the diameter of an end mill it will result in 16 times less deflection.
entries.frame_note: Same L^3 / D^4 law as Helical, from a vendor blog.

entries.verbatim: largest diameter possible, but the cutting edge length should be as short as possible and not more than three times the diameter
entries.frame_note: Router-bit vendor, wood. The sentence continues 'in a perfect world.' A selection rule for flute length, not a stickout de-rate and not a feed factor.

entries.verbatim: It is very critical that the 80% rule (at least 80% of the collet filled with tool shank) be followed
entries.frame_note: A holding rule. It bounds how far a short-shank tool can be pulled out for reach.

entries.verbatim: Use shortest CEL to achieve depth of cut
entries.frame_note: Troubleshooting remedy for TOOL BREAKAGE / Excessive Cutting Edge Length.

entries.verbatim: 3 x D Reduce feed rate by 50%
entries.frame_note: Depth of cut, not stickout. The LUT already carries it in ap_rule ('2xD reduce 25%; 3xD reduce 50%'). Searches for an Amana or Onsrud stickout de-rate returned only this depth rule.

DERIVED. Ratio of the printed extra-long wood cell to the printed standard 3-flute ball wood cell in the same chart. Ratios of the maxima: 0.875 (3/8), 0.889 (1/2), 1.0 (1/4 against 6 mm). The extra-long tools have a relieved neck and a short flute; at 3/8 in both tools are 4 in OAL, so the ratio is not a stickout effect. It is the only wood-router evidence found that a vendor prints a lower chip load for a long-reach tool. It is NOT a source for the repo's 0.88 share (that share acts on the load target, not the chip load).
